messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] getFragmentStarts
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On 11/01/2008, Christina <christin...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> What is the best way to extract fragment start/stop information from
> ufl /SnpInformation files?
> The getFragmentStarts function does not appear to be supported.

A UFL file contains the mapping (unit, fragment length), that is,
there it does not contain information about fragment position.  [The
UflSnpInformation class detects when you call getFragmentStarts() and
gives an error saying it is not supported.]

You have to turn to the NetAffx CSV file in order to get this data.
There is a class AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile that helps you deal with
NetAffx CSV files.  Note, that class is not a public class in the
sense that its API is well supported (have to minimize the public API
in order to have a chance to support the package).  Since the fragment
information in NetAffx CSV files are really "wrapped up" you have to
do some post-parsing yourself in order to grab the fragment start
position.  Have a look at readDataUnitFragmentLength() of
AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile, that is
readDataUnitFragmentLength.AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile(), to see how I
grab the start and the stop positions in order to calculate the
fragment lengths.

If you are looking for the *position of the SNP/CN probes*, then look
in the UGP file, which contains the mapping (unit, chromsome, physical
position).

Hope this helps

Henrik

messages.subject: Re: question about aroma
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cheryl,

first of all, please post all questions to the mailing list.

On Jan 21, 2008 10:27 PM,  <swe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I have several questions about aroma.
> Out-of-memory problem happened when I tried to process 4,235 CEL files
> by using R. (Affymetrix, type:HG-U133A&HG-U133B)

That is going to be interesting hear about [no sarcasm].  The largest
set I have ran this far was 600+ SNP arrays - memory-wise there is
basically no difference in running 10 arrays or 600+ (or 4,235)
arrays.

> Then, I found the aroma.affymetrix website.
> It mentioned that it can deal with unlimited arrays
> I think it's wonderful.
> After I browsed the website, there are some code (bg.adjustment,
> normalization and summarization) about human exon arrays.
> Can you give me some code example or advice since all I have are CEL
> files and the type of array is HG-U133A&HG-U133B.

The aroma.affymetrix package provides methods and classes for each
step in the pre-processing of typical Affymetrix microarray data for
most chip types.  What the package can do for your expression case is
to do the preprocessing up and until the point where have chip effect
estimates for each array and unit ("gene").  From there on you will
likely have to carry on with another package.

I recommend you to get started with setting up the directories and
files needed by aroma.affymetrix, because this is the same regardless
of chip type.  Then try to setup your so called CEL set, try out some
of the normalization methods (most of them are generic to any chip
type) available.  See the Page "Probe-level modelling" for how to fit
the log-additive model to your data, which I guess will just be:

plm <- RmaPlm(csN)
fit(plm)

You'll find all documentation online.  You might also find
"Elizabeth's column" (online) helpful as well.

Please also read the FAQ (online; everything available is online!) and
especially why it is slow in the beginning (you'll understand what I
mean when you get used to the package).

Maybe someone else can share a vignette on how to analyze expression
data?  Anyone who wish can contribute by adding a page online.

Hope this helps getting you started!

Henrik

>
> Cheers,
>
>
> Cheryl
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Yuan,
It looks like, based on your code, that you are using the cdf
distributed by Affymetrix. ('fromChipType' command will pull this one.)
This cdf has a number of EXTREMELY large probesets that consist of
control probes -- see previous discussions on this. I don't know that
others actually run out of memory using this cdf previously -- other
reports are just that it takes days, but I think they had quite large
machines--but that's likely the culprit.

The better solution -- even if you just want summaries per probesets
(exon) -- is to use the ExonRmaPlm function and choose mergeGroups=F AND
use one of the cdfs that we have distributed on the group pages that
group the probesets by transcript cluster (for example) and which also
get rid of these probes as a side product (e.g.
HuEx-1_0-st-v2,mainRx,A2007xxxx,EP.cdf, which includes all 'main' design
probesets). See the example code for an exon array analysis on the group
pages to see how to change your cdf and use ExonRmaPlm.
Best,
Elizabeth

Ok, it is obvious you've done your homework and found how to
circumvent the default behavior of not accepting ASCII CDFs.  The
intention of actually having this option is to leave a final resort to
turn to if you cannot get/generate a binary CDF for one reason or the
other.  However, you should always going to strive to use a binary
CDF.  Using an ASCII CDF is going to be painfully slow and consume
much more memory.

In your case you should be able to create a binary version of your CDF
by using convertCdf() in affxparser, e.g.

convertCdf(srcPathname, destPathname)

Note that the ASCII and the binary CDF will/must have the same
filename, e.g. HG-U133A.cdf.  So, make sure to put away the ASCII and
instead have the binary in
annotationData/chipTypes/HG-U133A/HG-U133A.cdf.  Do the same for the
HG-U133B.cdf.  If you do print(cdf) you will see if aroma.affymetrix
finds the ASCII or the binary CDF.

Names: 1102960533, 1102960569, ..., GSM9934
Time period: 2001-01-01 10:13:54 -- NA
Total file size: 78459.64MB
RAM: 6.21MB

So, the reason for the slow processing here is that the print()
function for an AffymetrixCelSet reports the time period of the first
and the last time stamp of the CEL files.  In order to figure this
out, it has to query and parse the CEL header of every single CEL
file.  This is something I've anticipated would happen, but I've
procrastinating optimizing it until it became a real issue, which it
now is.  Obviously, we do not want to do this if it takes to long.  I
can image adding an option that allows you to specify the maximum
number of arrays to report the time period, otherwise it will not be
reported.

> However, without the settings and checkChipType changes in step 2, the
> code complains about finding two chipTypes, so maybe there are indeed
> two types of chips.

The 'checkChipType' will scan *all* CEL files and assert that the chip
type is the same for all and match the name of the parent directory of
the CEL files, e.g. "HG-U133A" in your rawData/myDataSet/HG-U133A/
case.  This is to prevent mistakes, which obviously can happen for
many reasons.  As above, since this queries every single CEL file
having checkChipType=TRUE will take some time with your data set.

Which two chip types did it report - HG-U133A and HG-U133B?

You should never put CEL files of different chip types (think
different physical chip types that are produced by Affymetrix) in the
same directory.  Instead, in your case put the CEL files of the two
types in separated directories;

rawData/myDataSet/HG-U133A/
rawData/myDataSet/HG-U133B/

Then you have to treat to to sets of CELs as different data sets for
normalization, summarization and post-normalization.  It is first when
you get the final normalized summarized signals (chip effects) that
you can start thinking how to combine the two sets.  I know that there
are some discussion on normalizing the two chip types together using
common genes, but there is nothing available out of the box in
aroma.affymetrix.

The error message you get from running the quantile normalization
might be due to the fact that you mix up the two chip types.  I will
leave it for now until you retry doing it on the two chip types
separately, ok?

I will put it on my todo list to add additional speed optimization
methods for >1000 array data sets.  I already now have some ideas on
how to better cache CEL headers, since they are reread multiple times.

Hope this helps

The timestamp reported for each CEL file, is the timestamp found in
CEL file header.  Details: the timestamp is in the DAT header that is
part of the CEL v3 header that is part of the main CEL header - so
quite nested.  To the best of my knowledge, the DAT header is the one
generated when doing the scan/image analysis, so that is the data/time
reported.

Given the above, does the dates reported then make sense?  When you do
print(cs) on an AffymetrixCelSet 'cs', you will see the time span
covering the first to the last scan.

For CEL files containing chip effects and created by aroma.affymetrix,
the time stamps are reporting the creating date/time of the file.

> Is that the purpose of the command:
>  > timestampOn(verbose)
> that's on some of the example code?

No, that turns on time-stamps prefixes on the verbose/log messages.
This is unrelated to CEL file timestamps.
